Chapter Six: The Practice of Economy—Redefining Wealth and Work.
There’s this quiet satisfaction you get from making do with less—finding abundance, not in piling things up, but in really taking care of what you already have.
When most of us hear the word “economy,” we probably think of finances, stock markets, or maybe ledgers filled with numbers. But out in the woods, the meaning shifts.
Economy becomes something much simpler—using what’s at hand, wasting very little, and being amazed by how much you can actually accomplish with just a few simple tools and a bit of creativity.
Picture this: it’s late afternoon, and after a slow walk along the pond, the person who lives in the cabin sits down to mend a worn-out shirt.
The fabric is thin, and the stitches aren’t exactly perfect, but the act of sitting there, repairing instead of replacing, feels deeply grounding.
There’s no urge to throw something away just because it’s old, or to rush out and buy something new. Each patch, each seam, becomes a quiet act of care—a way of showing respect for the things that make up daily life.
Most of us have been taught to see wealth as something shiny and new—the latest phone, the trendiest clothes, or the biggest house on the block.
But out here, wealth looks different. It’s a stack of firewood that’ll keep you warm all winter. It’s jars of beans and berries lining the pantry shelves.
It’s a roof that never leaks when the rains come.
There’s real satisfaction in splitting your own firewood, growing your own food, or fixing a tool that’s seen better days.
That kind of satisfaction lasts a lot longer than the thrill of a new purchase.
Let me tell you about a neighbor who drops by one day, arms overflowing with vegetables from his garden.
He and the cabin-dweller swap stories and share a simple meal, laughing about the odd shapes of their harvest.
And you know, this exchange isn’t about who owes what, or who’s getting the better deal—it’s about helping each other out.
It’s a reminder that real economy isn’t about transactions; it’s about relationships.
Work, too, starts to feel different. Instead of pouring hours into chasing a paycheck, work becomes more purposeful—a way to meet real needs, to create, to share.
There’s a daily rhythm: tending the garden, splitting wood, patching up the cabin, or writing by candlelight.
Every little task becomes a chance to slow down and pay attention, to put care into the simplest things.
After a while, it starts to hit you: so much of what we call “work” is just a means to an end—a way to buy things we might not even need.
But if you can simplify your needs, if you learn to do more with less, suddenly you’ve got more time and energy for what really matters.
The woods offer a different kind of wealth.
Not something you can count in dollars, but something you feel—in freedom, in self-reliance, and in the quiet joy of simply having enough.
